This quarto tries to explain how to utilize `rlang` within `purrr`. There are some things we have to be aware about when we what to iterate using `purrr`. Building functions that use `tidyverse` functions make use of `{{}}` (curly-curly / embrace operator) and `.data[[]]` pronoun. In order to iterate over columns we need some type of strategy to be able to do this, and that strategy comes from having some knowledge about the `rlang` package.

```{r}
packs <- c("tidyverse", "rlang")
pacman::p_load(char = packs)
```

As an example:

```{r}
# Use the gss data:
dat <- forcats::gss_cat

# Set up a list of columns:
cols <- dat |> select(marital, relig, partyid, rincome) |> names() |> rlang::syms() |> set_names()

# Generate a function:
count_plot_helper <- function(df, var) {
    
    # Label and color palet:
    lbs <- rlang::as_label(enquo(var)) |> str_to_title() |> str_replace_all("_", " ")
    c_pal <- "steelblue"

    # Plot data:
    plot_data <- df |> 
        count({{ var }}, .drop = FALSE) |> 
        mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

    cli::cli_h1("Data: {.field {lbs}}")
    print(plot_data)

    # Plot
    p <- plot_data |> 
        ggplot(aes(x = prop, y = {{ var }}, fill = c_pal)) +
        geom_col() + 

        scale_fill_identity() +
        scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
        
        labs(y = lbs) + 

        theme_classic()

    cli::cli_h1("Plot: {.field {lbs}}")
    print(p)

    cli::cli_rule(left = "End {.field {lbs}}")

    # List return
    invisible(list(data = plot_data, plot = p, label = lbs))
}

# One variable first:
count_plot_helper(dat, marital)

# Then map:
res <- map(cols, \(v) {
    dat |> count_plot_helper(!!v)
}, .progress = TRUE)

```

- Is this actually a good way to do this? Well, not in all cases! This could be thought of as a `god function` - one function that does all! We could instead split it up into several:

1. first the `plot_data` function
2. then the actually `plot_function`.

- Note the key to sucess: i) first we use `names() |> rlang::syms() |> set_names()` to get our list object containing the cols we want to iterate over; ii) `!!` - the `bang-bang` operator inside our `map` call.

- We should also note the difference between a `purrr::map()` and a `purrr::walk()` call: `map()` can be combined with `<-` to assign an object with actual contents. `walk()` on the other hand is used for side effects, it delivers but throws away once delivered. To see this difference:

```{r}
# Use the gss data:
dat <- forcats::gss_cat

# Set up a list of columns:
cols <- dat |> select(marital, relig, partyid, rincome) |> names() |> rlang::syms() |> set_names()

# Generate a function:
count_prop_helper <- function(df, var) {
    
    # Label and color palet:
    lbs <- rlang::as_label(enquo(var)) |> str_to_title() |> str_replace_all("_", " ")
    c_pal <- "steelblue"

    # Plot data:
    plot_data <- df |> 
        count({{ var }}, .drop = FALSE) |> 
        mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

    cli::cli_h1("Data: {.field {lbs}}")
    print(plot_data)
}

# quick check using walk:
iwalk(cols, \(v, v_name) {
    dat |> count_prop_helper(!!v)
})

# Now assign:
map_test <- map(cols, \(v) {
    dat |> count_prop_helper(!!v)
})

walk_test <- walk(cols, \(v) {
    dat |> count_prop_helper(!!v)
})

# Show both objects:
map_test
walk_test

```

- That shown, we are good to go using `purrr::walk()` if we are looking for so called "side effects", i.e., saving a ggplot using `ggsave()`, writing a file using e.g., `readxl::writexl()`.

- We could even use `purrr` for loading libraries!

```{r}
# 1. restart R

libs <- c("tidyverse", "rlang", "cli", "fixest")
libs

# 2. load: purrr
library(purrr)

# Using map: keeps the output
libs <- map(libs, \(l) library(l, character.only = TRUE))
libs

# 3. restart R

libs <- c("tidyverse", "rlang", "cli", "fixest")
libs

# 4. load: purrr

library(purrr)

# Using walk: throws the output away
walk(libs, \(l) library(l, character.only = TRUE))
```
